claims.claim: Trigger finger, also called stenosing tenosynovitis, causes catching, locking, pain and stiffness in a finger or thumb.
Flexor tendons connect forearm muscles to finger bones and pull the fingers into a fist on the palm side. Pulleys hold tendons close to bone; the A1 pulley lies in the palm at the base of the finger.
A tendon may thicken or develop a bump, and the A1 pulley may thicken and narrow. This size mismatch prevents smooth gliding and causes catching or locking.
Symptoms may include a tender lump at the finger base, clicking or popping, and a finger stuck bent; stiffness and locking can be worse after inactivity or in the morning.
Many cases have no clear cause. Diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis are associated with greater likelihood; repetitive gripping or pinching is another association, not a universal cause.
Diagnosis usually uses symptom history and hand examination; X-rays or other tests are typically unnecessary.
Some cases improve on their own. Treatment options depend on symptoms and include reducing aggravating activities, a straight-finger splint, pain relief, and clinician-administered steroid injection.
Surgical release opens the A1 pulley to give the tendon room; surgery may be considered when symptoms are severe, other treatments fail, or the finger cannot be straightened.

Persistent symptoms or interference with daily activities warrant clinical assessment. A finger that cannot be straightened needs medical evaluation rather than forced manipulation. This is general education, not individualized treatment.

claims.claim: Tinnitus is perceived sound without an external source. Most cases are subjective, heard only by the affected person.
Sounds may ring, buzz, hiss or hum, occur in one or both ears or the head, and come and go or remain constant.
Hearing loss and loud noise exposure are linked to tinnitus; earwax or ear infection and some medications can also be associated. The exact causes are not fully understood.

One leading theory is that inner-ear damage changes nerve signals to sound-processing brain regions, including the auditory cortex. This is a theory, not a universal proven mechanism. The cochlea is the inner-ear structure that senses sound.
Tinnitus may affect sleep, concentration and mood. It is usually not a sign of a serious medical problem.

Evaluation includes an ear examination for earwax or infection, medical and medication history, and hearing assessment; specialist evaluation or imaging may be appropriate, especially for pulsating tinnitus.

Treating an identifiable underlying cause may reduce tinnitus. Hearing aids can help when hearing loss is present; sound therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy can reduce its impact, without promising a cure. There is currently no cure for tinnitus and no medication specifically for treating it.
Tinnitus that beats with the pulse needs urgent assessment. Tinnitus after head injury, or with sudden hearing loss, facial weakness or vertigo, warrants emergency evaluation.

claims.claim: Bursae are small fluid-filled sacs cushioning between bone and moving muscles, tendons or skin; bursitis means inflammation of these sacs.
Bursitis commonly affects shoulders, elbows, hips and knees.
A blow or fall, repeated motion, or prolonged pressure such as leaning on elbows or kneeling can cause bursitis.
Symptoms include dull aching pain, tenderness, warmth and swelling, often worse with movement or pressure; redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin.
A clinician examines the affected area; fluid sampling may test for infection or gout, and blood tests or scans may also be used.
Management may include rest from aggravating activities and pressure, wrapped ice packs and pain relief; many cases settle within a few weeks.
Infection-related bursitis may need antibiotics. Steroid injections may reduce swelling but are not given if infection is the cause; aspiration may ease symptoms.
Fever or chills, inability to move the joint, very severe pain, or symptoms persisting or worsening after 1 to 2 weeks of self-care warrant medical assessment.
Padding during kneeling and regular breaks from pressure-producing activities may help prevent recurrence.

claims.claim: Acute otitis media is a middle ear infection with swelling and fluid trapped behind the eardrum; it is different from an outer ear canal infection.
The ear canal ends at the eardrum; the middle ear lies between the eardrum and inner ear. The malleus, incus and stapes transmit sound vibrations toward the inner ear.

The eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the upper throat, supplies air, drains fluid and helps maintain pressure. In children it is smaller and more level; swelling or mucus during a cold can impede drainage.
Bacteria or viruses can cause middle ear infections, often after an upper respiratory infection.
Symptoms can include ear pain, fever, fussiness, ear tugging and difficulty sleeping; symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.
Clinicians ask about symptoms and examine the eardrum with an otoscope; a red bulging eardrum can indicate infection. Pneumatic otoscopy can check eardrum movement for fluid.
Otitis media with effusion is fluid in the middle ear without infection; fluid may remain after an infection. Persistent fluid can affect hearing.

Many middle ear infections improve without antibiotics. Clinician-directed watchful waiting or delayed prescribing may suit mild cases; severe or persistent cases may need antibiotics. Treatment depends on clinical assessment.
Pain or fever relief should be selected with a healthcare provider for the child's age and size; no prescription doses or universal antibiotic recommendation are given.

Medical care is needed for worsening symptoms, ear discharge, hearing loss, fever of 102.2°F (39°C) or higher, or symptoms lasting more than 2 to 3 days. A baby under 3 months with fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs medical attention right away.
Recommended flu and pneumococcal vaccines, clean hands and avoiding secondhand smoke help reduce risk, but do not guarantee prevention.

factualInfographic.description: How lichens form a fungus-photobiont partnership with a layered thallus, three growth forms and dual reproduction
factualInfographic.sourceNote: USDA Forest Service https://www.fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/beauty/lichens/about.shtml and https://www.fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/beauty/lichens/biology.shtml; British Lichen Society https://www.britishlichensociety.org.uk/learning/what-is-a-lichen. claims.claim: A lichen is a stable symbiotic partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner (photobiont): green algae and/or cyanobacteria.
The photobiont photosynthesizes and supplies sugars (carbon) to the fungus; the partnership is thought to be a mutualism.
The fungus is the dominant partner and gives the lichen most of its characteristics, including thallus shape and fruiting bodies.
About 90% of lichens use a green-algal photobiont; some lichens have both green algae and cyanobacteria.
Lichens have no roots, stems, leaves, waxy cuticle or vascular tissue; they absorb water and nutrients from air and rain.
The thallus is layered: an outer cortex of tightly packed fungal cells, an algal layer beneath it, and a medulla of loosely packed threadlike fungal filaments.
When a lichen is wet, cortex cells become transparent and the algal layer's color shows through; green algae often make a wet lichen bright green.
Rhizines are fungal filaments from the medulla that attach the lichen to its surface; they do not move water or nutrients like roots.
Some foliose lichens attach by one central holdfast (umbilicate lichens, such as rock tripe).
Three main growth forms: crustose (pressed against the surface like a crust), foliose (leafy, with distinct upper and lower sides), fruticose (hair-like, shrubby or cup-like).
The fungus produces spores from fruiting bodies; a new fungus must find a compatible photobiont partner.
Lichens also reproduce vegetatively: soredia are granules of algae and fungi intertwined for dispersal, isidia are vegetative outgrowths, and fragments can grow into new thalli.
By protecting its photobiont, the fungus lets lichens live in dry, sunny places where algae alone could not, recharging with occasional rain.
Lichens absorb pollutants such as heavy metals and sulfur from the air, so scientists use them to monitor air quality; old man's beard (Usnea longissima) is an air-pollution indicator.
Lichens are not mosses: mosses are plants with leaf-like structures, while lichens are not plants.

Evaluation includes clinical assessment and comparing blood pressure at the ankle and arm with an ankle-brachial index.

claims.claim: Southern mole cricket is Neoscapteriscus borellii, formerly Scapteriscus borellii.
Adults are brown, with enlarged digging forelegs, forewings longer than the pronotum and hindwings extending beyond the abdomen; body length is 25–32 mm.
Neoscapteriscus has two blade-like dactyls on each foretibia; in N. borellii they are separated at the base by at least half a dactyl basal width.
Mole crickets force loose soil aside with strokes of the enlarged forelegs and spend nearly all their lives underground.
Southern mole cricket habitat includes moist sandy or mucky open areas such as lawns, fields and pond or stream margins.
The species is native to South America and introduced to the southeastern United States.
Males call with a low ringing trill from a horn-shaped burrow opening; specialized calling burrows augment and project sound skyward, attracting flying conspecifics including females.
A generalized Neoscapteriscus calling burrow contains an opening horn, constrictions, a bulb, a turn-around and surface/deep tunnels.
Eggs are gray-brown, bean-shaped, laid in underground chambers; nymphs resemble smaller wingless adults.
Southern mole crickets are largely carnivorous, though omnivorous; they mostly eat other insects.

A generalized insect nervous system has a dorsal brain connected to a ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia; thoracic ganglia innervate legs and wings. This is a generalized schematic, not a measured species dissection.
One generation per year is typical except in south Florida, where there can be two; eggs are laid in spring and large nymphs or adults overwinter.

claims.claim: Atychiphobia means intense fear of failure; this is an established descriptive phobia name, not a separate diagnostic code.

claims.claim: The urinary tract includes two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder and a urethra; kidneys produce urine, ureters carry it to the bladder, the bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it outside.

Burning urination, urgency, frequency, lower abdominal discomfort and sometimes blood in urine are symptoms; smell or dark urine alone does not establish UTI.
Catheters, impaired bladder emptying, pregnancy and menopause can increase risk.
Clinical assessment uses symptoms and history and may include urine testing; urine testing is not always needed.

Fever or chills, back pain below the ribs, blood in urine, pregnancy, or rapid worsening warrant urgent medical advice; new confusion, marked drowsiness or difficulty speaking warrant emergency help.

claims.claim: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated disorder affecting the central nervous system: brain and spinal cord; immune attacks damage myelin around axons and may damage axons themselves, disrupting communication.
Myelin is the protective coating around nerve fibers; demyelinated lesions can occur in the brain and spinal cord and can be seen with MRI.
Symptoms vary by person and lesion location: fatigue, visual problems, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness or stiffness, and balance problems can occur.
Some people have relapses and remissions; others experience progressive worsening. The course varies and cannot be predicted from a single illustration.

The exact cause is unclear; genetic susceptibility and environmental factors contribute, and smoking and prior Epstein-Barr virus infection are associated with increased risk, not certainty of disease.
No single test diagnoses MS: a neurologist combines history and examination with MRI and sometimes spinal fluid or other tests, excluding other causes.
There is no current cure. Disease-modifying therapies can reduce relapses and slow progression for appropriate patients; treatment depends on disease type and individual needs.
Corticosteroids may speed recovery from a relapse but do not change the long-term course; physiotherapy, tailored exercise, fatigue management and symptom medicines can help.
Sudden arm weakness or numbness, sudden vision loss or sudden balance problems can signal stroke and require emergency medical help; do not assume they are MS.
MS-like symptoms can have other causes and should be checked by a clinician; general education is not diagnosis.

Gallstones can block the opening of the pancreas; gallstones and heavy alcohol use are common causes, while some medicines and other conditions can also cause it.
Symptoms include sudden persistent severe upper abdominal pain that may spread to the back, nausea, vomiting and fever.
Sudden severe persistent abdominal pain needs urgent medical evaluation; severe pain spreading to the back, fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing warrants emergency care.
